title: A Resource Estimation Model for the Hardware-Software Co-Design of Distributed Quantum Architectures
authors: Raymond P. H. Wu, Chathurika Ranaweera, Sutharshan Rajasegarar, Ria Rushin Joseph, Jinho Choi, Seng W. Loke
abstract: In distributed quantum computing (DQC), executing monolithic quantum circuits across multiple interconnected quantum processing units (QPUs) requires dedicated communication qubits to generate and distribute entanglement. Because the number of physical qubits within a QPU is finite, a trade-off emerges where allocating more communication qubits increases the capacity of quantum channels for concurrent non-local operations, but reduces the number of computational qubits available for local gate operations. Distributed quantum compilation routinely ignores this channel capacity, while hardware architects lack a method to determine it prior to quantum circuit partitioning. Moreover, scheduling entanglement on demand introduces severe latency, whereas pre-fetching exposes stored pairs to decoherence. We propose an economic order quantity model from perishable inventory theory to optimize the trade-off between entanglement distribution latency and the time cost of decoherence. The resulting estimate is driven by algorithmic demand and physical constraints, offering a dual application for the hardware-software co-design of high-performance DQC: for hardware architects, it gives the optimal allocation of dedicated communication qubits in static heterogeneous architectures; for compiler developers, it gives the optimal number to reserve dynamically in homogeneous architectures.
summary: This paper introduces an economic model based on perishable inventory theory to optimize the allocation of communication qubits in distributed quantum computing architectures. It quantifies the critical trade-off between minimizing network latency and mitigating decoherence losses. The resulting framework offers actionable guidelines for both hardware designers setting static resource budgets and software compilers managing dynamic reservations.
main_problem: The core problem is optimizing resource allocation in Distributed Quantum Computing (DQC) by balancing the trade-off between entanglement distribution latency and decoherence time.
main_result: The authors propose an optimal number of communication qubits ($N_{comm}^*$) derived from minimizing a total system cost function, providing guidance for both hardware architects and compiler developers.
method: They adapt an Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) model from perishable inventory theory to quantify the time cost associated with entanglement distribution delays versus decoherence penalties.
model_or_system: The study models DQC across interconnected Quantum Processing Units (QPUs), where qubits are split into computational and communication roles. The optimization is governed by a total system time cost function incorporating latency, physical execution costs, and decoherence rates.
key_observables: Total system time cost $C(N_{comm})$, optimal number of communication qubits ($N_{comm}^*$), entanglement demand rate ($R_{QPU}$).
important_parameters: Coherence time ($T_2$), algorithmic fidelity threshold ($F_{th}$), network latency costs ($C_{lat}, c_{lat}$), and the QPU demand rate ($R_{QPU}$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes continuous consumption of entanglement resources, using time-averaged rates; a proactive cutoff strategy is employed to manage decoherence by discarding pairs exceeding a maximum usable lifetime.
figures_summary: Figure 1a illustrates the trade-off between latency cost and decoherence cost versus $N_{comm}$, while Figure 1b shows how the optimal $N_{comm}^*$ changes as a function of the fidelity threshold ($F_{th}$).
paper_structure: The paper develops the mathematical model by defining the total time cost, deriving the unconstrained optimum, and then incorporating physical constraints from coherence time to yield the final piecewise minimum estimate.
why_interesting: While focused on DQC resource management rather than fundamental AMO physics, the underlying principles of managing finite resources under decoherence (like inventory control) are highly relevant to designing robust quantum communication protocols in trapped ion or superconducting qubit systems.
